criterion_notes.c1: Examines household and neighbourhood access to water (shared piped connections, unmetered municipal standposts, wells, water tankers) and sanitation (public, CBO-managed, and private toilet blocks, hanging latrines, and drain cleaning) in two informal settlements in Mumbai.
criterion_notes.c2: Satisfies BOTH the plain wording and the narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type mechanism reading of Criterion 2. Under the plain wording, it analyses legal, municipal, and community governance of urban water and sanitation. Under the narrow rule-type reading, it directly examines concrete legal and administrative rules governing service access: (1) statutory slum notification requirements under the Maharashtra Slum Areas (Improvement, Clearance and Redevelopment) Act, 1971, governing settlement eligibility for basic amenities; (2) the 1 January 1995 residency cut-off rule and documentary proof requirements for legal municipal water connections; (3) administrative burdens, bureaucratic unresponsiveness, and informal payments/political mediation required even for legally eligible pre-1995 residents in notified settlements to obtain shared MCGM/BMC water connections; (4) municipal enforcement raids cutting off water connections and requiring proof of legality to reconnect; and (5) user-charge/tariff rules, operating-hour restrictions, water shut-offs, and informal lock-and-key access rules governing private, CBO-run, and chawl toilet blocks.
criterion_notes.c3: Primary qualitative socio-legal/ethnographic empirical study based on nine months of fieldwork in two informal settlements in Mumbai, involving participant observation and repeated interviews with residents, municipal staff, NGOs, and community groups. Qualitative socio-legal studies are explicitly eligible for the systematic review.
criterion_notes.c4: Reports multiple access outcomes including water connection attainment and disconnection, standpost and tanker water availability and regularity, toilet seat availability across settlements, operating hours/night closures, user-fee affordability, and physical exclusion of specific groups (post-1995 or non-notified residents and daytime garment workers).
criterion_notes.c5: Clearly identifies population and units of analysis (households/residents and neighbourhoods in two Mumbai informal settlements: non-notified Rafinagar with ~4,000 households and notified Khotwadi with ~2,000 households), rule-type exposures, access/exclusion outcomes, and comparative qualitative ethnographic case study design.

evidence_quotes.quote: The research involved participant observation of different areas in both neighbourhoods, extensive and repeated interviews with a cross-section of people from both neighbourhoods, and interviews with municipal staff, non-governmental organizations, and community groups working on sanitation and water.

While most residents in Khotwadi have a degree of secure water access through unmetered municipal standposts, metered group connections and wells, most of Rafinagar’s residents face profound difficulties and incur high expenditures for water and/or time and effort in collecting water.

An informal settlement must be notified (declared) as a slum under the Maharashtra Slum Areas (Improvement, Clearance and Redevelopment) Act, 1971, for it to legally qualify for the provision of basic amenities such as water, toilets, streetlights and drainage.

For example, water cannot be legally provided to residents who arrived in the neighbourhood after 1 January 1995, meaning that these residents are doubly excluded through both the legality of the space and the time of inhabitation (pre-1995). Residents estimate that only 1,500 out of a total of 4,000 households in Rafinagar can prove pre-1995 residency.

Even though Khotwadi is a notified informal settlement and Shobha and her neighbours are pre-1995 residents, obtaining a shared water connection as per the policy of the Municipal Corporation of Greater Mumbai (MCGM or BMC) has been a fraught process. Encounters with unresponsive municipal officials often force residents, even when they are legally entitled to a shared water connection, to approach their representatives for what can also be a long, frustrating process.

Both legal and illegal connections were cut during the raids without adequate alternative provision, destabilizing provision previously gained, and Rafinagar was thrown into an even deeper water crisis than before.

raw_response.exposure: Statutory slum notification status (Maharashtra Slum Areas Act, 1971), pre-1 January 1995 residency cut-off and proof requirements for municipal water, municipal administrative hurdles/political mediation and anti-theft disconnection raids, and toilet user-charge/tariff and local access rules (public, CBO, and private blocks).
raw_response.outcome: Household and neighbourhood access to piped shared water connections, standposts, and tanker water; toilet block availability, night-time continuity, user-fee affordability, water disconnection, and exclusion of non-notified/post-1995 residents and garment workers.
raw_response.population_and_sample: Residents and households (as well as municipal staff, NGOs, and community groups) in two informal settlements in Mumbai, India: Rafinagar (unauthorized/non-notified, ~4,000 households) and Khotwadi (authorized/notified, ~2,000 households); units of analysis are residents/households and neighbourhoods.
raw_response.rationale: This nine-month comparative ethnographic study in two Mumbai informal settlements (Rafinagar and Khotwadi) empirically examines how formal legal eligibility rules (slum notification under the 1971 Act and the pre-1995 residency proof cut-off), municipal administrative practices and enforcement raids, and local tariff/access rules for toilet blocks shape household and community access, affordability, continuity, and exclusion in water and sanitation services. It meets all inclusion criteria under both the plain and narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type readings of Criterion 2, and as a qualitative socio-legal empirical study it is eligible for the systematic review's mechanism synthesis.
raw_response.study_design: Comparative qualitative ethnographic study (nine months of participant observation and interviews in two neighbourhoods)
